messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Eleanor had spent months telling herself that the trip to the former war zone was over, that the work she had done there as a relief worker belonged to another life, but the memory never stayed where she put it. It would force its way into her mind at random moments, not as a full story but as pictures: a stretch of shattered street, a doorway half collapsed, a child’s face in profile, the blur of dust hanging in sunlit air. She noticed that it felt strangely alien, as if it belonged to someone else rather than to her, and that odd distance only made it more unsettling. Since the deployment she had come to believe that if she thought about what she had seen she would not be able to handle it, and that belief made her flinch away from anything that might bring it back. Yet the very effort to keep it down seemed to make it push harder against her mind, arriving uninvited when she was trying to prepare notes for council meetings or sit through an evening alone.

What frightened Eleanor most was how easily the world now seemed to press against that memory. Heavy breathing in a crowded corridor, the sharp bang of a door slamming in city hall, even a burst from a car backfiring outside her apartment could jolt her into a sudden state of alarm. In those moments the pictures returned at once, and the scene in her mind felt less like recollection than intrusion. A sound of heavy breathing on a busy committee floor could carry her straight back to the tense, waiting silence of the field clinic; a bang in the street could flood her with the same stark images of impact and wreckage. She found herself pulling away from stairwells, from loud meeting rooms, from places where she could not control the noise, because she had come to believe the world was a dangerous place and that danger could appear without warning. The more the memory leapt in, the more she watched the environment for signs of it, listening for breathing, scanning for sudden sounds, bracing before she even knew what had startled her.

That sense of danger fed back into the way Eleanor held the memory itself. She said it did not feel like her own life, only a set of vivid snapshots that had somehow attached themselves to her, and that detachment seemed to confirm her fear that something fundamental in her had been damaged. She worried that she would never be able to feel normal emotions again, because outside of the sharp fear and tightening dread there was little else she could reliably access. When she tried to think through what had happened, the images appeared first, and with them came the conviction that she had somehow crossed into a place from which ordinary feeling did not return. Then the thought of the event became another threat, something she avoided by burying herself in council work, staying late at meetings, and steering conversation away from anything that might touch on conflict or aid work. Even so, the pictures would still arrive, and when they did she would once again be looking for the sounds that set them off, as if preparing for the next blow.

Over time, the cycle narrowed her life. Eleanor kept attending her city council duties, but she sat closest to the door and grew tense whenever a microphone cracked, a folder slammed, or someone came in breathing hard from climbing the stairs. She began leaving receptions early, skipping crowded public forums, and arranging her days so she would not be caught in small enclosed rooms where a sudden bang might echo. Colleagues noticed that she seemed more distant, less patient, and she herself knew that the effort to stay ahead of the next trigger was exhausting. What had started as an attempt to avoid being overwhelmed by the memory had become a way of living inside constant alertness, because every sound seemed capable of summoning the same alien pictures and every picture seemed to prove that the danger was still near. By the time she finally sought help, it was not only the war-zone scenes that troubled her but the life she had built around not encountering them. She came in worried that if she kept avoiding the memory she would remain trapped in this narrowed, watchful version of herself, yet she was equally afraid that facing it directly would leave her unable to cope.

violation_explanations: No paragraph clearly states that triggers/reminders cause the memory to intrude; the vignette shows triggers occurring alongside intrusions, but not a direct trigger-to-memory causal link in the same paragraph.
No paragraph clearly shows triggers leading to negative appraisals; the sounds and cues evoke alarm and memories, but they are not described as causing the patient's negative beliefs or appraisals.
No paragraph clearly states that negative appraisals drive the intrusive memory; her beliefs about not coping are linked to avoidance, not to the memory intrusions themselves.
No paragraph clearly shows negative appraisals causing triggers/reminders to become salient or frequent; the beliefs lead to avoidance, but not to triggering cues.
No paragraph clearly states that the intrusive memory produces the negative appraisals; the memory is described as unsettling, but not as the cause of her beliefs about damage or inability to cope.
No paragraph clearly states that the memory produces the triggers/reminders; the cues are presented as external stimuli that summon the memory, not as something generated by the memory.
